The mother of two children who had been in isolation during Covid wanted to create an unforgettable experience for her daughter Michele, who was turning three, and her son Liam, who was turning one. After much brainstorming, we decided to create a Mickey and Minnie themed party that catered to both children's ages. We paid attention to every little detail to ensure that the party would be a huge success. We created beautiful backdrops that were perfect for the theme, and made sure that the favors, cakes, and sweets were all in line with the theme. From the Mickey and Minnie shaped cookies to the Minnie Mouse headbands, every detail was meticulously planned and executed. It was such a fun theme party to create, and we had a blast doing it! This birthday party was designed to celebrate the special day of a young boy named Liam, who had a great passion for cars. His mother contacted us for assistance in creating a unique and memorable party theme that would be perfect for her son's interests. We discussed several ideas and agreed on a car race theme that would ca
ChIJ0_y556LBwokRJDpDxfpVTU0.about: “As children, we all live in a world of imagination, of fantasy, and for some of us that world of make-believe continues into adulthood.” My name is Valy and I am originally from Brazil but now I live in Westchester with my husband, our three children, and our dog, Diego. Being raised by a single mother with three siblings I did not have a birthday party until my surprise sweet sixteen. After that, the spark was lit and I told myself that when I had children, I would make sure that every single birthday felt as special as that first one was for me. Over the years, I have discovered a real passion for finding creative and beautiful ways to make parties and events special. I get so much joy and satisfaction from seeing the smiles on people’s faces when they enjoy my work! After years of bringing my personal touch to my friend's birthday parties, weddings, showers and other events, I finally made my passion into my business. I will work with you to elevate any gathering; from small dinner parties to life's biggest celebrations. You can expect handcrafted creativity, elegant attention to detail, and heartfelt originality in everything I do. I can't wait to help you plan your next special event!

ChIJ2R9jRSDrwokRY_93pZd3Z-I.home: Timeless Elegance Overlooking the Hudson, Perfect for Every Occasion. 723 S. BROADWAY | TARRYTOWN, NEW YORKâ A historic property on more than 25 acres Located in Westchester County, the Belvedere Estate is a unique property, built on more than 25 acres. Featuring beautiful period details from the 1920s, the estate is comprised of a main house and several smaller buildings scattered across the grounds. A wooded area and bluff overlooking the broad Hudson River and Tappan Zee Bridge offer a variety of beautiful and idyllic views. Built as early as the 1910s, the Belvedere was originally part of Philipsburg Manor, a 90,000-acre property and one of the richest landholdings in America. It was built by Florence and Casper Whitney and purchased in 1928 by Dr. Philip Gillette Cole, where it was renamed Zeeview. The house at Zeeview sat comfortably overlooking the broad Hudson River and the "Tappan Zee." Here, the Coles built several more buildings on the property, including the Agora House and the Studio, and displayed their extensive collection of American Western art, later placed in the Gilcrease Museum in Tulsa, Oklahoma. After Coleâs death, the estate was acquired by Samuel Bronfman of the Seagrams Whiskey family. The property was renamed Belvedere, after the Bronfmanâs main residence in Toronto. In 1972, Belvedere became the center of operations for the Family Federation for World Peace and Unification. Today, the Belvedere Estate is a beautiful event and meeting space â the ideal setting for receptions, wedding ceremonies, meetings, office parties, location and film shoots, or any other occasion where a beautiful interior and exterior setting is desired. Contact us at info@thebelvedereestate.com

Number 1 Firehouse 1904-1924 Did you know Colonial Flower Shop is the home to the Original Firehouse of Ronkonkoma circa 1904-1924? In 1903, a group of brave men became firefighters, fighting a fire in a local hotel. In 1904, the firefighters officially formed a group known as the Ronkonkoma Hook & Ladder Engine Co. No. 1 from 1904 to 1924. John W. Cleary was the company's first chief. The Company originally protected an area of five square miles, including Ronkonkoma, Lake Ronkonkoma, Centereach, Lakeland, Lake Grove, Holbrook, Holtsville and Farmingville. Dues of 15 cents per month supported the organization as well as donations and social functions run by the company. The firehouse was often rented to various groups who showed films and held dances. The most successful form of fund raising, however, was the Firemans Fair, which were very popular social gatherings. The townspeople allowed the Company to purchase its first fire apparatus. It was a horse drawn vehicle which carried one hundred feet of hose. Lake Ronkonkoma Fire Department has since moved to it's new home on Portion Road in Ronkonkoma. the name has been changed from Ronkonkoma Hook & Ladder Number 1 to Ronkonkoma Fire Department. ChIJ9VXHK2mpwokRlvHSaCflh2g.about: The distinguished grandeur of a hilltop Gilded Age mansion, breathtaking views of Hudson Valley sunsets from terraced patios, and acres of lush gardens combine to make Le Chateau an unforgettable destination for weddings and special events. High on a hillside in South Salem, New York, Le Château was commissioned by J.P. Morgan in 1907 as a gift for his pastor and friend, the Rev. William S. Rainsford. Originally called Savin Rock, the country retreat was designed by Atterbury & Atterbury, prominent architects of the day. The tudor-style mansion of brick and stone would be virtually impossible to duplicate today, both financially and in craftsmanship. The rooms are paneled in American chestnut, a wood no longer available, cherry and oak. Huge chestnut beams are found throughout, and all of the woodwork was hewn and detailed by hand. Grand staircases and massive stone fireplaces are further reminders of a gracious era long past. Under new ownership, Le Chateau has launched the next chapter of its storied history. Fairfield Catering Group purchased the property in Fall 2016, and invested $10M in a comprehensive facility update and expansion befitting the property’s grand legacy. The venue’s updated lobby and cocktail spaces preserve the history of the mansion, with every antique detail and surface inspected and refreshed. The Farm On Main started the same way a lot of meaningful things do… not as a business plan, but as something built for family. Tom and Jessica Scangarello, Long Beach Island locals and owners of Bay Avenue Plant Company, purchased this 20-acre property in 2016 to support their growing business. What began as a space for composting and family farming slowly turned into something more. They renovated the iconic “Little Blue House” on the property, creating a warm, welcoming home for their family. Today, that same space lives on as The Farmhouse, where our brides spend their wedding day mornings. As their friends and family started celebrating life’s biggest milestones here, it became clear this place had a different kind of energy. It felt special, like it needed to be shared. In September 2023, The Farm On Main officially opened its doors to the community, and since then, it has become a space where couples near and far can experience something that’s increasingly hard to find: a wedding venue that feels entirely their own. Commissioned by distinguished Atlanta attorney William A. Wimbish as a residence befitting his family’s social status, The Wimbish House was designed by W. T. Downing, one of Atlanta’s most notable architects. Known for homes that were innovative and sophisticated, Downing was the preferred architect for Atlanta’s stylish elite, and he later designed many of Atlanta’s most prestigious public buildings, including The Church of the Sacred Heart of Jesus , Trinity United Methodist Church , First Presbyterian Church , and Lupton Hall at Oglethorpe University . Designed in the eclectic French Renaissance Revival, or Chateau-esque, style, this lovely Victorian-era home is distinguished by steep gables, intricate detailing, and massive stone masonry ornamentation. Located at 1150 Peachtree Street and now a beloved Midtown icon, The Wimbish House is lovingly restored and is designated a national, state and city landmark. The Wimbish House is owned by The Atlanta Woman's Club , and funds from its operation are used to support the Club’s charitable activities. Together, these neighboring properties offer not only a premier golfing and event experience but also a deep connection to the rich and evolving history of the Rossville community. The story begins in the mid-18th century, when the area was known as Old Blazing Star, later shortened to Blazing Star, named after a well-known local tavern that served travelers on Staten Island’s western shore. In the early 1800s, the area was renamed Rossville to honor Colonel William E. Ross, a prominent landowner, entrepreneur, and statesman. Colonel Ross was a man of great accomplishment. In 1832, he fought alongside Abraham Lincoln in the Black Hawk War, and by 1860, he was one of eleven delegates from Pike County, Illinois, who cast votes for Lincoln at the Republican Nominating Convention. Throughout his life, Ross helped shape American civic life founding the first bank in his area, operating three riverboats, a general store, a flour mill, and serving as postmaster. He was also instrumental in the founding of the Republican Party. On Staten Island, he built a grand mansion styled after Windsor Castle, locally known as the Ross Mansion or Ross Castle. Most of them lived in the Belmar area. Some of them would stop by a local bar in Belmar called Pats Tavern. The owner of the tavern was a man from Newark, NJ named Pat Joyce. The veterans became close friends with Pat Joyce. The men would bring their wives to the tavern for steak and lobster on Saturday nights. They wanted to play cards and have a club. The men would play in the rear of the tavern for a short time. One of the men went to look around for a site where they could possibly build a building and play cards. They found that land on West Hurley Pond Road in Wall Township. A retired man from New York lived in the woods on the property. He lived in a small wooden house. He had food and supplies dropped off at the end of his driveway. His building was next to a natural spring, which he used for water, on the property. He made an agreement with the man who offered to buy the property. The agreement was that he would sell 4 acres of the property with life rights. The man went back to Pats Tavern and told the other men of the property. They agreed and a short time later the man died. The property next to the newly purchased property went up for sale. ChIJMWM_QmuGwYkRq59u8ryfPyo.about: About the River Queen: A Waterfront Wedding Venue in New Jersey A Waterfront Venue for Weddings and Private Events in Brielle, NJ Nestled along the Manasquan River in Brielle, the River Queen is a waterfront wedding venue in New Jersey and a distinctive private event venue on the Jersey Shore. The River Queen is part of the Bogan family legacy, rooted in Brielle, New Jersey since 1930 with the founding of Bogan’s Basin. What began as a working waterfront gradually grew into a way of sharing the experience of being on the water with others. In 1988, that idea became the River Queen, a custom Mississippi River boat replica built in North Carolina. After her maiden voyage of over 700 miles along the intracoastal waterway, she arrived in Brielle, where she continues to cruise along the Manasquan River, Point Pleasant Canal, and Barnegat Bay. Today, the River Queen is a place where people come together to celebrate, offering a welcoming setting for weddings and private events on the Jersey Shore, with the character of a historic vessel and the comfort of a modern waterfront venue in New Jersey. This attracted the attention of up and coming chefs & restaurateurs such as David Bouley, Tom Colicchio and Danny Meyer, who began picking up produce from the farm's Greenmarket stand on a regular basis. Other chefs caught wind of what the farm was offering and began requesting that the farm try growing unique crops from then hard to obtain imported seeds. The farm answered these requests, word began to spread, and before long Blooming Hill had a small but loyal group of wholesale customers, and was delivering weekly to restaurants in New York City and the surrounding area. ChIJP4bd2c4p6IkRX2EIB5co0lI.about: LEARN ABOUT OHEKA CASTLE A RICH AND VIBRANT HISTORY Celebrating 100 Years of History from 1919 to 2019 A century ago, financier and philanthropist Otto Hermann Kahn built OHEKA CASTLE in the middle of a 443-acre plot on the highest point on Long Island in Cold Spring Harbor for an estimated cost of $11 million ($158 million in today’s currency). At the time of its construction, the French-style chateau was—and still is today—the second-largest private residence ever built in America. During the Gilded Age of the 1920s, Kahn used the 109,000-square-foot, 127-room estate as a summer home where he hosted lavish parties and regularly entertained royalty, heads of state, and Hollywood stars. After Otto Kahn died in 1934, the estate changed hands several times, serving as a retreat for New York sanitation workers and a government training school for Merchant Marine radio operators. In 1948, the Eastern Military Academy bought OHEKA, bulldozed the gardens, subdivided the rooms, and painted over the walls. After the school went bankrupt 40 years later, OHEKA stood abandoned, except by vandals who set numerous fires over five years. In 1984, developer Gary Melius purchased OHEKA and the remaining 22 acres that surrounded the estate and began the painstaking challenge of restoring the Castle to its original grandeur. Villa Russo’s story began in 1954, when brothers Frank and Joseph Russo, sons of Italian immigrants, opened Russo’s Pizzeria in Richmond Hill, Queens. What began as a neighborhood pizzeria was built around family recipes, warm hospitality, and a commitment to serving the local community. Through their dedication, hard work, and attention to detail, the Russo brothers expanded their small neighborhood pizzeria to a full-service restaurant, gaining a reputation for producing the highest quality Italian cuisine in Queens, New York. As the requests for their unique recipes poured in and their loyal following grew In 1975, the Russo Family officially entered the catering business by building a banquet hall adjacent to their existing restaurant and named it Il Palazzo di Villa Russo. Which held its first wedding reception in 1977, and the Russo brothers, Frank and Joseph, discovered that their true passion was catering to the special occasions in the lives of their patrons. ChIJRbK1iLhvu2sRZm85kf4yJtk.home: Weddings and events at our historic farm & barn, in the heart of New York's Hudson Valley. The Phelps Riverside Farm is a fourth generation, family owned, NY State & National Historical Landmark in Walden, New York, on the Wallkill River. It features a rustic, hand-built and raised Dutch Barn as the centerpiece, the 18th century Dubois-Phelps farmhouse, and fifty acres of land. Our farmland features areas that are well-suited to a multitude of event types; from barn weddings and ceremonies, to corporate retreats, to any large or intimate celebration or event. It is also an ideal place to plan unique themed photoshoots.
ChIJRbK1iLhvu2sRZm85kf4yJtk.about: Known formerly as the Dubois-Phelps House, the original farmhouse dates back to the late 1700’s, being built in Walden, New York, in the Hudson Valley. In 1851, it was purchased and renovated to its current iconic Greek Revival style by Nathaniel Dubois. In 1922, the property was purchased by Sam Phelps where it has remained in the family for four generations. in 1997, the Phelps House was added to the National Register of Historic Places, a sub-division of the National Park Service. It is currently owned by Sam Phelps’ great-grandson, Sam Phelps IV, alongside his wife Melissa and two daughters. The property just celebrated its 100th Anniversary as the Phelps Riverside Farm. Today, the property also serves as an event venue used to host iconic barn weddings, ceremonies, parties, corporate retreats, and more.

ChIJSZq1sjZawokRxwogbYlwP3E.about: Originally a residential block, the Dumbo neighborhood developed into a major factory area in the late 1800s-early 1900s. Soon, the manufacturer Edward H. Cole established it as one of the most industrial neighborhoods in the city. This brought in William Taylor & Sons Columbian Iron Works on Adams and Water Street, a sign making company, a brass foundry, a two-story machine shop and storage facility for E. W. Bliss and Phillips, Doup & Company. Many of these factories in the area were demolished to make way for the Manhattan Bridge. Luckily, the building at 155 Water Street wasn’t affected by the construction of the bridge and has a long history of manufacturing ironworks and other materials. In 1905, Edward Cole used the factory to make steam fittings then leasing out the property to Phillips, Doup & Company, who built steam heaters. Cole sold the building in 1920 to L&H Stern, manufacturers of smoking pipes and accessories. The company used the lower floors as offices and the upstairs as the production space. The simple brick facade, articulated by segmental openings and projecting lintels and sills, marks 155 Water Street as an example of the American round arch style. Additionally, the slow-burning mill construction and history make it an amazing representative of American factory architecture – contributing greatly to the character of the Dumbo Historic District.

ChIJVUCnEuxYwokRct0vRgeYkyg.about: In 1920 the Harold Pratt House was designed and erected for Mr. and Mrs. Harold Irving Pratt by the famous New York architect, William Adams Delano, of the firm Delano and Aldrich. The prestigious firm was sought out from the wealthiest of families including the Rockefellers, Astors, Vanderbilts and Whitneys for their coveted architectural styles. Only the best materials available were used in constructing the house which is reputed to have cost over a million dollars in 1920. Mr. Harold Irving Pratt was the youngest of eight children. His father, Mr. Charles Pratt, merged Pratt Astral oil with John D. Rockefeller’s Standard Oil of New Jersey during the latter part of the 19th century. The current Rockefeller Ballroom was the Pratt family’s formal drawing/living room. At Mrs. Pratt’s insistence it was square, being modeled after a room she had seen in Ireland. It is decorated with pine paneling and beautiful chandeliers each of whose crystals are completely unique. It was also Mrs. Pratt’s wish to use the hand-painted Venetian type doors for the entrance to the Library and the drawing room, although the architect demurred that they did not fit with the English architecture. These charming doors are still gracing the entrances to the Rockefeller Ballroom and Rubin Library. The Pratt Family gave three paintings of themselves seated with the original furnishings. ChIJZ3VO7K4z3YkR9q7UHA2WeGQ.about: Father Jim Rooney is a priest, chaplain, and pastoral minister dedicated to serving people of all faiths, backgrounds, and life experiences. Born and raised in Glasgow, Scotland, he is one of ten children in a close-knit family. His early formation in faith and community continues to shape his inclusive and compassionate approach to ministry today. Father Jim entered Scotus College Seminary in 1987 and was ordained a Roman Catholic priest in 1994. He holds a bachelor’s degree in Philosophy and Theology from St. Patrick’s Pontifical University in Maynooth, Ireland. His early ministry included serving in the Diocese of Glasgow, followed by eight years in New York City as a hospital chaplain at St. Vincent’s Catholic Medical Center and Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, where he supported patients, families, and medical staff through some of life’s most profound moments. While he remains deeply committed to his priesthood, Father Jim stepped away from the institutional Roman Catholic Church, guided by his personal convictions, particularly regarding mandatory lifelong celibacy. He now lives in Beacon, New York, with his husband. He is a member of the International Council of Community Churches, www.citiministries.org and www.icccusa.com .We provide service throughout the United States. ChIJc4OCE9mHwokR7YVJpknRwvo.about: Built around a single arch on Willis Ave. “ We didn't set out to be a landmark. We just kept showing up. ” The arch started small — a weekend experiment with dahlias and chicken wire that was supposed to come down by Monday. It didn't come down. It became a reason people stopped their cars, pulled out their phones, and found us. Every spring, we rebuild it from scratch. The frame is the same welded steel we've used since year two. What changes is the season and what we're feeling. April means ranunculus and white. June means peony and rouge. By autumn it's amaranthus in shades that match the leaves on the maples out front. The arch is temporary by design. It wilts, and that's the point. Permanence would make it decoration. Impermanence makes it alive. Behind every stem that leaves Diva Flowers is Maky, our founder. She started in 2014 with one simple idea: flowers should feel personal, not packaged. She's still the one who chooses, cuts, and composes — with a specific space and a specific person in mind. Over a decade later, that hasn't changed.

Photos that bring the memory of your day flooding back. The big laughs. The look across the room. The tears. The moments that no one else caught. That’s what I do for you. Located at the northern end of the two ponds in Setauket, the park of twenty-four acres includes a circular walkway around the upper pond, the home of the last miller in Setauket, a simulated mill house with a working water wheel, the recently restored Setauket Post Office, Hap’s barn, scenic trails, and the Bates House, a venue available to rent. Built between 1804 and 1808, Boscobel was originally the dream house of wealthy Loyalists. By the 1950s, after falling into disrepair, it was demolished. Preservationists saved as many architectural fragments as possible and reassembled them fifteen miles north, where the Neoclassical mansion was restored back to—and even beyond—its original grandeur. Boscobel opened as a nonprofit museum sixty years ago. Built between 1804 and 1808, it was originally the dream house of wealthy Loyalists. By the 1950s, after falling into disrepair, it was demolished. Preservationists saved as many architectural fragments as possible and reassembled them fifteen miles north, where the Neoclassical mansion was restored back to—and even beyond—its original grandeur. Boscobel was saved as a beautiful piece of art. Now an esteemed Historic House Museum containing one of the finest collections of decorative arts from the Federal period, Boscobel offers admission to 68 acres of our grounds, featuring lush gardens and a woodland trail. Located in the heart of the Hudson Valley, Boscobel directly overlooks Constitution Marsh toward the U.S. Military Academy at West Point, showcasing dramatic views of the Hudson River. Jennifer Carlquist is a 30-year museum professional celebrating historic landscapes, buildings, and interiors; their contents; and contexts; as powerful tools for community engagement. ChIJp1C2eAD7ZUARS-2oe0qX-28.title: Forest Park Highlights - Oak Ridge : NYC Parks
ChIJp1C2eAD7ZUARS-2oe0qX-28.home: Official Website of the New York City Department of Parks & Recreation Find A Park > Forest Park > Highlights > Oak Ridge Standing in a grove of red and black oaks, Oak Ridge is located on the crest of the Harbor Hill Moraine (a mass of rock formed by glacial movement) at the southwestern corner of Forest Park, overlooking Jamaica Plains. A turn-of-the-century golf house, Oak Ridge now serves as the Forest Park administration headquarters, the home of the Queens Council for the Arts, and a community center. During the acquisition of Forest Park in 1895, landowner David Leggett sold this parcel to the Brooklyn Department of Parks. This two-story structure was built in 1905 in a Dutch Colonial Revival style as a facility for the Forest Park Links. It was designed by the firm of Helmle, Huberty, & Hudswell, who also designed the landmark Williamsburgh Savings Bank (now home to HSBC bank) in Brooklyn. Located near the first tee, the house held lockers for men and women. The Forest Park Links opened as a 9-hole golf course in 1901, and expanded to 18 holes in 1905. In the early days after its expansion, professional golfers used the course, caddies earned 25 cents per game, and many of the numbered holes had names such as “Camelback,” “Cabbage Patch,” “Bunker Hill,” “Lover’s Lane,” “Old Glory,” and “San Juan Hill,” named for Teddy Roosevelt’s erroneously attributed charge in the Spanish-American War (1898-99). San Juan Hill, the eighth hole, also became popular as a site for sledding in the winter. The 110-acre, par 67 course was modeled after Scottish links and is still known as one of the City’s most challenging golf courses. In 1906, a second, more exclusive golf house opened near Myrtle Avenue and 80th Street at the house of wealthy French landowner Edward Bourcier. Bour

ChIJq6oaL9rIwokRQ1kb0IAte4U.about: The 187-year-old, three-level structure was built by William Nelson- Peekskill lawyer, Congressman and friend to Abraham Lincoln. Its first use was as a grocery store in 1838. The Peekskill telegraph office was then located here in the 1860s. A small stage, built on the 3rd floor in 1870, was identified as the “Dramatic Hall.” The street level retail store, known as Durrin Brothers, provided hardware supplies starting around 1880. This business became Kurzhals Brothers Hardware in 1920. Later on, the Capital Glass Company operated here in the 1970s and 80s. This emblematic building had been abandoned for about 20 years and fallen into disrepair until 2012, when Mr. Gabriel Arango, who already owned several buildings in downtown Peekskill, purchased the 15,200-square-foot building with a unique vision for Peekskill Central Market, including completely renovating an 1870-era theater on the third floor that can seat almost 100 people. “It’s unique. I saw the potential to convert it into an attraction for the community. I want to make a contribution to the progress of the city. The main attraction is the location,” explained Arango, a Colombian-born businessman, resident of White Plains and proprietor of EZ Housing. “Many people tried to buy this place before, but they failed to fulfill the dream. ChIJqxnu-5vVw4kRuWXDzHh5Xk8.about: Our story begins long before there were greenhouses. For generations, the Patterson family has farmed this land, adapting with the seasons while staying true to time-honored practices. What follows is a look at the moments that shaped Patterson Greenhouses into what it is today. The Patterson family roots stretch back to the early 1800s. In 1834, Frank and Austin Patterson built the farmhouse that still stands today, originally for their father, John C. Patterson Sr. The home has seen remarkably few changes and remains a living piece of Patterson history. For generations, the Patterson farm was centered around dairy cows and, before that, potatoes. Hay and straw were always part of farm life, grown to support the livestock. These traditional farming practices laid the foundation for what Patterson Greenhouses would later become. The Pink Elephant first appeared around 1960 as a gift when the family’s grandfather served as Republican Mayor of Howell. Painted pink at Grandma’s request, it became a local landmark — first for the dairy farm, and now for Patterson Greenhouses. After years of weather damage, it has been lovingly restored to watch over the farm once again. In 1987, the dairy cows were sold, marking a major shift in the farm’s future. ChIJuzQ00nJW0AcRvPpWTU_5_oU.about: My culture runs through everything I play. I grew up in the Bronx, and back then every place I walked into had its own music. When I entered a bodega I heard bachata, merengue, and salsa . I step outside the street and hear hip-hop and rap being played on the stoop. I go visit my mom in the beauty parlor and hear ballads ( Canciones Romanticas ) with everyone singing along badly and having a great time. That’s what I’m after when I play: the song you heard everywhere back then, and the memory that comes with it. When asked how I feel now that Latin music has hit the mainstream, all I can say is POR FIN! (Finally!) . People missed out on a lot of great music from the late 90s and 2000s. It’s only going to grow, and I love playing those records live and singing along with the room. My job now is to put the old ones on and say, “Hey this was fire back in the day and still is now.” I started in 2016, playing small birthday parties and local bars around Brooklyn. Nothing glamorous, but those rooms taught me the most important thing: how to read a crowd and keep people with you. Since then I’ve worked my way up to big private parties, galas, fashion shows and brand pop-ups. The list keeps growing, but the job hasn’t changed. h2: In a world saturated with color, black and white photography whispers a quieter truth.
ChIJz8eWujOVwokRKvbhdhxcDKc.home: Weddings aren’t a show to be staged—they’re stories told through honest moments and quiet connections. With a love for film and black and whites, we capture the raw beauty that can’t be scripted or checked off a list. We're Rob and Kelly Villetto, a husband-and-wife wedding photography team with roots based in the Hudson Valley. Our approach blends documentary-style storytelling with an eye for the unscripted—capturing real, unposed moments as they naturally unfold. We believe the best images happen when you're not aware of the camera. Our couples often tell us, "I didn’t even know you were there"-and that’s exactly the kind of presence we aim for. Quiet, observant, and always ready to catch the in-between moments that tell the real story of your day. Our editing style is clean and timeless—less saturated, with a deep appreciation for black and white imagery and the nostalgic feel of film photography. We're inspired by honest emotion, natural light, and the unique rhythm of every couple we work with. We photograph weddings across the Hudson Valley, from NYC to the Catskills, and everywhere in between. If you're looking for wedding photographers who stay in the background but never miss a beat, we'd love to connect. I shoot film on wedding days because it sees differently. It slows things down, demands intention, and embraces imperfection. It’s not always sharp, not always perfect—and that’s exactly why I love it. There’s depth in film. Texture. A kind of honesty you can’t replicate. The grain, the softness, the subtle tones—they all remind me that the beauty in a moment isn’t in how polished it is, but in how real it feels. ChIJz8eWujOVwokRKvbhdhxcDKc.about: I’m Rob Villetto—wedding photographer, dog person, and someone who’s happiest with a camera in hand and fresh air around. I shoot weddings all over the Hudson Valley, NYC, and the Catskills with a documentary style that favors real over perfect. I’m not into loud people, forced poses, or turning your wedding into a production. I’d rather blend into the background, capturing the stuff you didn’t even know was happening. That’s the good stuff. I love film photography, black and white images, and keeping things simple and honest. When I’m not photographing weddings, I’m probably outside—somewhere quiet—with our dogs, my wife, and daughter, and zero talk about politics. Kelly’s known for her quick wit, love of yoga and smoothies, and a deep obsession with old, charming homes full of character. She finds beauty in the details—the way light hits a weathered window or how a quiet moment lingers just a little longer. Her photography style is patient and thoughtful, capturing moments with a natural, easy charm. She lets the day unfold without force, focusing on what’s real. When she’s not behind the camera, she’s probably on her yoga mat, blending a smoothie, exploring vintage spaces—or just hanging out with our daughter and the dogs. We've been in some cool places. I am devoted to creating celebrations that are not only beautiful, but deeply meaningful and truly unforgettable. My creative journey began as a stay-at-home mom, eventually evolving into a successful career in corporate event coordination, where I designed, managed and hosted high-level experience-driven experiences for leading organizations. Following a life-altering brain tumor diagnosis and recovery, I felt a profound calling to pursue what had always lived within me — transforming spaces and creating beauty with my hands. At the ripe young age of 61, I founded Lifestyle Event Designs, proving that it is never too late to step fully into your purpose. Central to my design philosophy is the art of reimagining and repurposing forgotten treasures.
